options.a: The first of the two insureds dies
options.c: The second of two insureds dies

distractorExplanations.a: Paying at the first death describes a first-to-die joint life policy, not survivorship (second-to-die) coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: Survivorship life pays on death, not disability; disability protection comes from a waiver of premium rider or DI coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Reaching a maturity age triggers endowment or policy maturity, not the survivorship death benefit.

options.a: Use of any provider with lower cost sharing for in-network care
options.b: Payment of a deductible before any preventive office visit is covered
options.c: Filing claim forms for reimbursement after paying providers in full
options.d: Selection of a primary care physician and referrals for specialists

distractorExplanations.b: HMOs cover preventive care with little or no cost sharing, and the ACA bars a deductible for in-network preventive visits.
distractorExplanations.a: Freedom to use any provider with better in-network cost sharing describes a PPO, not an HMO's gatekeeper model.
distractorExplanations.c: Paying providers and filing for reimbursement describes indemnity plans; HMO members pay copays and providers bill the HMO.

options.a: Employer against catastrophic claim levels above specified thresholds
options.b: Employees against out-of-pocket costs above the plan's annual maximum
options.c: Plan participants if the employer becomes insolvent and stops paying claims
options.d: Insurer against catastrophic losses it cedes under a treaty contract

distractorExplanations.c: Stop-loss is a contract that reimburses the employer, not a guarantee to participants if the employer becomes insolvent.
distractorExplanations.b: The out-of-pocket maximum is plan design that protects employees; stop-loss reimburses the self-funded employer.
distractorExplanations.d: Ceding losses under a treaty is reinsurance of an insurer; stop-loss protects a self-funded employer plan.

options.a: Standard premiums with a flat extra for an elevated health risk
options.b: Higher premiums due to a table rating for medical history
options.c: Lower premiums due to favorable health/lifestyle characteristics
options.d: Average premiums reflecting the typical risk found in the insured pool

distractorExplanations.d: Average premiums for typical risk describe the standard class; preferred risks pay less than standard-class insureds.
distractorExplanations.a: A flat extra premium is a substandard rating tool for elevated risk, not a feature of the preferred class.
distractorExplanations.b: A table rating with higher premiums describes a substandard (rated) class, not preferred.
